# The Moral Ledger: Who Paid and Who Was Erased {#sec-5-09}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act V — The Open Era · 1769–2025
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** What does California's ascent cost, and who bears that cost?

**The answer.** It costs a specific set of people a specific set of things, and
the book can name them. Every phase of California's ascent had an excluded class
that made the system work and was denied its returns: Indigenous Californians,
Chinese railroad labour, the sterilised, farm workers, offshore factory workers,
contractors, moderators, data labellers. The chokepoint always externalises its
cost downward.

**The mechanism.** The cost side of all three mechanisms, accounted for in one
place. This chapter is not a moral appendix — the preceding chapters have
carried the excluded throughout, as the briefs require. Its function is to show
the pattern as a series, because the recurrence is the evidence that it is
structural rather than incidental.

**The key fact.** The pattern is not a series of unrelated injustices. In each
generation the same structural position is occupied by a different population:
legally at arm's length, economically indispensable, and absent from the balance
sheet. That consistency is the argument.

**The human anchor.** A ledger, literally. The chapter should be structured as
an accounting document, because the book's method is bioeconomic and this is
where the surplus and its sources are finally set against each other.

**Excluded voices.** The chapter's entire subject. The discipline is to write
each group as agents with names, actions, and resistance — not as a catalogue of
victims. Every entry should include what these people did, not only what was
done to them.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that exclusion is structural rather than
incidental to California's model by showing the same position filled by a
different population in every generation across two hundred and fifty years.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

This chapter is laid out as an accounting document, with surplus in one column
and its sources in the other, because the book's method is bioeconomic and this
is where the two are finally set against each other.

It is not a moral appendix. Every preceding chapter has carried its excluded
population as part of the structural argument, and this one assembles them in
sequence, because the recurrence is the evidence. In each generation the same
structural position is occupied by a different group: legally at arm's length,
economically indispensable, and absent from the balance sheet. That consistency
is the argument, and it is what distinguishes a pattern from a list of
injustices.

The entries run in order. Indigenous Californians, through mission labour, the
state-sanctioned killings of the Gold Rush decade, and dispossession. The
Chinese workforce of the Central Pacific, their 1867 strike, and the Exclusion
Act that followed their work. The people sterilised under the 1909 law, cited as
a range with its basis. Farm labour from the ranchos through the Bracero
programme to the United Farm Workers — Steinbeck's subjects from Act III, and
their own organising. Offshore manufacturing, from Fairchild's Hong Kong
assembly through Nike's contract factories to electronics assembly across Asia.
And contract and platform labour: drivers, warehouse workers, content
moderators, and data labellers, with employment classification as the mechanism
that holds them at arm's length.

The chapter's discipline is to write each group as agents rather than victims.
Every entry includes what these people did — struck, litigated, organised,
published, won cases that changed American constitutional law — and not only
what was done to them. A ledger of passive suffering would be both bad history
and bad argument.

The Introduction's four questions are answered here in aggregate: who controlled
the inputs, who captured the surplus, who was excluded, and how the system
reproduced itself.

The cost was never hidden. It was accounted for elsewhere. This is where it is
accounted for here.

:::

::: {.chapter-question}
What does California's ascent cost, and who bears that cost?
:::

This chapter is an accounting document.

Every preceding chapter has carried its excluded population as part of the
structural argument, because a system's costs are not a moral appendix to its
operation — they are how it operates. What this chapter does is set the entries
in sequence, because the recurrence is the evidence.

The claim is not that California produced a series of unrelated injustices.
Every country has those. The claim is that one structural position has been
occupied continuously for two hundred and fifty years by a succession of
different populations, on identical terms: legally at arm's length, economically
indispensable, and absent from the balance sheet.

## The four questions

The Introduction proposed reading history the way an ecologist reads a food
chain. Who controls the inputs. Who captures the surplus. Who is excluded. How
the system reproduces itself.

Applied across the whole book, the answers are consistent enough to be boring,
which is the point. The inputs have been land, then capital, then credentials,
then attention, then compute. The surplus has been captured by whoever held the
passage. The system has reproduced through an institution that certifies the
people who endow it.

And the excluded have changed nationality every generation while occupying the
same slot.

## The entries

**Indigenous Californians, from 1769.** Enumerated in mission registers,
compelled into a labour system they could not leave, and subject to a population
collapse in the mission districts that the missions' own burial records
document. Then, after 1848, dispossession under a new sovereign, state-funded
militia expeditions, an 1850 statute permitting the arrest of Indians deemed to
be loitering and the indenture of Indigenous children, and eighteen treaties
negotiated and never ratified. What they did: they fled, they revolted at San
Diego in 1775 and in the Chumash rising of 1824, they litigated for a century
and a half, and the Muwekma Ohlone and other nations are still pressing federal
recognition claims using the mission registers as evidence of continuous
existence.

**Chinese railroad labour, from 1865.** At peak the large majority of the
Central Pacific's workforce, paid less than white workers, unhoused by the
company, killed in numbers it did not record. What they did: they struck in June
1867 — several thousand men in the Sierra, demanding pay parity and shorter
hours in the tunnels — and were broken by having their food cut off. They laid
ten miles and fifty-six feet of track in a single day in 1869, a record that
stands. Then exclusion in 1882, and the communities that remained litigated:
*Yick Wo* in 1886 established that a law neutral on its face but administered
with an unequal hand violates equal protection, and *Wong Kim Ark* in 1898
established American birthright citizenship. Both are still cited constantly.

**The sterilised, from 1909.** Overwhelmingly poor, disproportionately Mexican
and Black, committed to state institutions and operated on without meaningful
consent, in numbers that made California responsible for roughly a third of the
recorded national total. The law stood until 1979 and documented coerced
sterilisations in California institutions continued well beyond it. The state
established a compensation programme for survivors in 2021.

**Farm labour, continuously.** A hundred-year sequence of recruited and
discarded workforces: Chinese, then Japanese — dispossessed by the Alien Land
Law of 1913 and then incarcerated in 1942 — then Filipino, whose status was
changed in 1934 specifically to make them excludable, then Mexican under the
Bracero programme and after it. What they did: the Filipino and Mexican workers
of Delano struck in 1965, and the United Farm Workers won contracts that had
eluded organisers for sixty years.

**Offshore manufacturing, from 1963.** Fairchild's Hong Kong assembly plant,
then Korea and Taiwan, then the shoe factories of Indonesia and Vietnam, then
electronics assembly across Asia. Young women, in every case, paid a small
fraction of the American wage, employed by contractors so that the brand held no
liability.

**Platform and contract labour, from the 2000s.** Drivers and couriers
classified as independent contractors. Warehouse workers. Content moderators in
Manila, Nairobi, and Austin, employed by outsourcing firms, doing documented
psychological damage to themselves at a fraction of engineering pay. Data
labellers in Kenya and Venezuela classifying material selected because it is
disturbing. What they did: they organised, they litigated, they won a
classification ruling in California in 2018 and legislation in 2019, and they
were overridden in 2020 by a ballot measure on which the platforms spent more
than two hundred million dollars.

## The structural observation

Read the entries against each other and the pattern is not thematic. It is
mechanical.

In each case the work is essential to the enterprise. In each case the worker is
held at arm's length by a legal device — a mission's spiritual jurisdiction, a
labour contractor, an exclusion statute, an offshore subsidiary, an independent
contractor classification. In each case the entity capturing the surplus has no
formal relationship with the person generating it. And in each case, when
resentment about the resulting inequality builds, it is directed at the
workforce rather than at the arrangement.

That last step is the one Act II chapter 11 documented most fully, and it is the
reason the mechanism is stable. A grievance aimed at the excluded costs nothing
to satisfy. A grievance aimed at the chokepoint costs everything, and the
chokepoint has lawyers.

## Against the passive voice

There is a way of writing this chapter that would be a catalogue of suffering,
and it would be both bad history and a weaker argument.

Every group in the ledger acted. The strikes, the lawsuits, the organising, the
flight, the record-keeping, the century-long persistence of communities that
were supposed to disappear: these are not footnotes to the story of what was
done to people. They are the story, and several of them changed American law
permanently in ways that now protect everybody.

The two most cited equal protection cases in this list were brought by Chinese
laundrymen and a Chinese-American cook's son. The modern doctrine of
discriminatory enforcement and the modern rule of birthright citizenship are
their achievements, won against a state that had specifically excluded them from
testifying in its courts thirty years earlier.

A ledger of passive suffering would miss that entirely.

## What the record cost

There is a second column in this ledger and it is the one Act I chapter 1 opened
with.

We know a great deal about the mission system because the Franciscans kept
registers. We know less about what the people in those registers thought,
because they did not keep any. We know the Central Pacific's construction costs
to the dollar and cannot say with confidence how many men died building it,
because the company recorded the first and not the second. We know the
sterilisation figures only through institutional files that were compiled for
administrative purposes and through the retrospective work of scholars who went
and counted.

The asymmetry is not an accident of survival. It is a consequence of who
employed scribes, and it means that every chapter of this book is better
documented on the side of the people who captured the surplus than on the side
of the people who generated it.

Historians work around this and readers should know it. When this book gives a
precise figure for a land grant and a range for a death toll, the difference in
precision is not a difference in importance. It is a difference in who was
counting.

The excluded were not only denied the returns. They were denied the record, and
then the absence of the record was used to suggest the returns had not been
denied.

## What the accounting is for

Not guilt, and not reparation, though a reader may reasonably arrive at either.

The accounting is for accuracy. California's ascent is generally described as an
achievement of enterprise, and it was. It was also financed, at every stage, by
a transfer from a population that had no standing to refuse, and that transfer
does not appear in the accounts because the accounting was done by the
beneficiaries.

The cost was never hidden. It was recorded somewhere else — in mission burial
registers, in coroner's findings the railroad did not compile, in institutional
files, in contractor payrolls, in the terms of service of firms with no
employees.

This chapter is where it is entered on the same page as the surplus.
